newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU budget deal sound, but no panacea - economists.
newsitem.headline: EU budget deal sound, but no panacea - economists.

text.p: The budget pact hammered out in Dublin is probably the best compromise deal Germany could have hoped for, but only time will tell whether it will really fulfil the task of giving strength to Europe's single currency.

Economists on Monday broadly welcomed the European Union's agreement to continue to strive for fiscal discipline once the euro is launched in 1999 and to impose sanctions and fines on those governments which fail to keep a firm hand on spending.
But they said that while the agreement was a step in the right direction, it did not in itself guarantee a strong Euro.
"Stability does not depend on rules, sanctions and fines," said Armin Kayser, economist at SBC Bank. "In the end it depends on the commitment to take all these things seriously."

It was worries like this that prompted German Finance Minister Theo Waigel to propose the stability pact last year, fearing that governments might otherwise relax consolidation efforts as soon as they had made the entry grade for the euro.

Within the framework of the pact, countries have now pledged to keep their budgets as balanced as possible or in surplus. They also promised to use get-out clauses that would allow excess spending only when absolutely necessary.
But analysts said it had yet to be seen whether these commitments, enshrined in a political declaration issued after marathon talks, were really shared at a practical policy level.
There were indications, based on comments from this weekend's summit meeting, that big differences remained at Europe's core -- particularly between France and Germany.

"Looking at comments from (French president Jacques) Chirac and Waigel this weekend it is clear that very substantial differences of view remain," said Thomas Mayer, chief economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.

Referring particularly to France's tendency to see currency depreciation as a useful economic tool, which Germany opposes, he added: "The old question remains of what kind of euro do we want. The stability pact has not resolved this."
Tight fiscal conditions might also simply shift tensions to other areas, such as wage or monetary policy, Mayer said.

The efficacy of the pact itself would depend on which of the European Union's 15 nations joined the single currency in 1999 and how restrained they were in using escape clauses in the pact which would allow them to overspend without penalty.

Under the terms of the deal, a country may run an annual deficit of more than three percent of gross domestic product if its spending is buoyed by a circumstance beyond its control or if its economy suffers a severe recession.

An economic contraction of two percent in one year is incontrovertibly defined in the pact as a special circumstance. But nations with a small fall in growth may also plead for clemency, especially if the contraction exceeds 0.75 percent.
A sharp fall in growth, possibly exacerbated by fiscal tightfistedness, could undermine the pact early on, by sparking a wave of calls for special case treatment, analysts said.

This meant it was particularly important that would-be member nations had their budgets genuinely under control before they melded their currencies into the euro, rather than using tricks or one-time special measures to squeeze their deficits.
"If we see exemptions being granted right from the start then it will be a bad sign for the strength of the currency," said Norbert Braems of BZW in Frankfurt.

But despite its potential problems, the Dublin agreement had achieved an important success in demonstrating to the public that Europe was still firmly resolved to creating the single currency and to making it a success, analysts said.
This was particularly important for Germany, where nervous citizens are wary of surrendering their cherished marks for the unknown quantity of a shared European currency.
"The marketing aspect of this agreement plays a fairly big role," Kayser said. "Finally, Waigel can now claim evidence that the euro will be as hard as the mark."
